```
completion(prompt, *, model?="default"|"smol"|"slow", system?=None, schema?=None) → handle
    Returns at once; `.wait()` returns text (parsed with `schema`). Stateless, no tools/history.
    JS: ONE trailing object — `h = await completion(prompt, { model, system, schema })`; without `await`, `.id` is undefined. `.wait()` returns a Promise.
await judge(state, questions, *, images?=[path | ImageContent, …]) → `{id: answer}`
    Typed judgment over one `state` (non-empty str | JSON object | JSON array). Every question sees the same state and is answered independently: batch independent questions into one call. Cheap and fast (TypeSafe when credentialed, else the tiny/smol chat model); prefer over `completion()` for classification, yes/no, ranking. Two or more states → `judge_batch`, never a loop of `judge()`.
    `questions`: `{id: q}` where q is one of
      `{type: "choice", instructions, criteria: {label: rubric | None, …}}` → `{choice, probabilities: {label: p}, confidence}` (≥2 labels)
      `{type: "bool", instructions, criteria?: {true?: str, false?: str}}` → `{bool: P(yes)}`
      `{type: "score", instructions, criteria: [lowest, …, highest]}` → `{score, probabilities: {"0": p, …}, confidence}` (≥2 levels; score is the probability-weighted level index)
    JS: ONE trailing object — `await judge(state, questions, { images })`.
judge_batch(states, questions, *, concurrency?=32, retries?=1, min_ok?=1, intent?=None, images?={key: [path | ImageContent, …]}) → JudgmentBatch
    Images accept local paths or embedded `ImageContent`; batch attachments map each state key to its list (array inputs use zero-based index keys). Image requests skip candidates without image support, never silently drop images, and fail if no compatible judge remains.
    Same `questions` over every state (`{key: state}` or a list keyed by index), run and owned by the host — it outlives the cell. `concurrency` is capped at 32. `intent` is an optional nonempty progress/job label (default `"Judging"`). Returns at once; pull settled items in bounded slices across cells: `await b.drain(timeout?)` (seconds; omitted waits for the next item) → `[(key, item)]` settled since the last drain (`[]` on timeout or once the run is done; `item.ok` → `item.answers`, else `item.error`; item failures never raise); `async for k, item in b.drain_iter(timeout)` until timeout or completion; `b.status()` → `{id, intent, done, total, failed, cost, running, model?, elapsedS, error?}`; `b.results()` → `{key: answers}` so far; `b.failed()` → `{key: error}`; `b.cancel()`; `b.close()` cancels it if running and releases it. `drain()` raises only when the run died wholesale (no judge, fewer than `min_ok` answered, or cancelled). `b.id` is an async job id: completion auto-delivers a summary, the `wait` tool (not kernel `wait()`) blocks when you have nothing else to do, `judge_batch.attach(id)` re-creates the ref after a reset.
    JS: ONE trailing object — `b = await judgeBatch(states, questions, { intent, concurrency, retries, minOk, images })`; `await` every `b` method except `drainIter`, which you iterate with `for await (const [k, item] of b.drainIter({ timeout }))`; `drain` yields `[key, item]` arrays; `await judgeBatch.attach(id)`.

# org-chart

The chart is the sole grant authority. Humans edit org facts (positions,
reporting lines, role assignments, hire/move/leave); the compiler derives
effective capabilities deterministically. Nobody edits a capability directly.

- Same schema, same compiler, both extremes: a deep multi-compartment
  hierarchy and a single position holding a single WireGuard key are both
  just charts. Depth is recursion with a bound (32); cycles refuse.
- No implicit inheritance: positions hold explicit roles. What you see is
  what compiles — no subgroup alignment to untangle later.
- Clearance attributes gate role capabilities per member; missing attributes
  skip the grant **with a recorded reason**, never silently.
- Every grant carries provenance (`via_role`, `via_position`) answering
  "why do I hold this cap?" — the read-only view the console renders.

displayContent.text:
# catalog-routing

Pure request routing over nested catalogs: `routing/DATA-MODEL.md` as code.
No I/O, no network.

- `catalogs/compliance` — control tags → OSCAL controls → candidate plugin
  operations (`oscal/TAG-TAXONOMY.md`; `oscal/` JSON is authoritative).
- `catalogs/ui` — component support per renderer target
  (`docs/DROP-IN-SPEC.md` §2.1; the sealed `json_render` blob is authoritative).
- `catalogs/models` — provider/model selection over a caller-supplied registry
  (the live `chat_router` catalog is authoritative; this crate only matches).
- `decide` — allow / refuse (naming the missing capability) / needs-approval
  (root: two humans, mirroring the `approvals/` crate).

[hackathon/README.md#31BE]
1:# Etched in Schema
2:
3:**An identity that acts — and can prove what it did.**
4:
5:Etched in Schema is a self-contained 3tched identity — the living embodiment
6:of a business subsidiary — that turns a business goal into deployed,
7:working infrastructure. Every action it takes is authorised against its
8:capabilities, bounded by compliance rules, recorded as a tamper-evident
9:receipt, and anchored on a blockchain so anyone can verify *who did what,
10:under what authority, and what actually happened* without trusting the agent
11:or its operator.
12:
13:Built for the Meta Model API hackathon (Startup Track — judged on a working
14:product) by Jeremy Hobson, founder of 3tched.
15:
16:> **The method is the blob — the identity acts only through 3tchedFS.**
17:> Every method is a plugin schema sealed into a blob. The identity's own
18:> 3tchedFS mount projects each sealed method as a typed file
19:> (`operations/<plugin>/<method>/call`); the identity writes arguments there,
20:> the bridge admits it by kernel identity, checks the exact capability, commits
21:> and returns a receipt. No MCP, no direct API calls, no `ovs-*` commands.
22:> Every new method built here follows: **logic in this repo → plugin
23:> registration → sealed blob → operation file in the mount → call → receipt.**
24:> The UI is derived from the same blobs: screens from sealed schemas, actions
25:> call the same sealed methods and show their receipts. Each plugin is a
26:> **schema feed** (schema + committed state, streamed); state has one writer
27:> (MutationEngine) and is archived as receipts, Btrfs snowball snapshots and
28:> vectors.
29:> See [`docs/DEV-CYCLE.md`](docs/DEV-CYCLE.md).
30:
31:## Why
32:
33:AI agents can reason about goals, but they rarely have a durable identity,
34:verifiable permissions, accountable execution, or the ability to build and
35:operate real systems. On-chain artifacts have the mirror-image problem: a
36:contract address or a content hash proves something exists, not that it came
37:from an accountable actor following permitted steps. That missing link
38:between artifacts and accountable, authorised actors is what keeps businesses
39:from trusting both autonomous agents and Web3.
40:
41:Etched in Schema closes that gap from both sides: every on-chain artifact
42:points to the identity and authorised operation behind it, and every
43:operation points to the artifacts it produced, with the history anchored
44:on-chain.
45:
46:## Goals — the new, judged product
47:
48:The identity platform (3tched) existed before the hackathon and is used only
49:through its interfaces. The **new development, built and judged here**, is:
50:
51:1. **Compliance routing** — a business's requirements become an OSCAL profile;
52:   OSCAL tags route each request and each requirement to the components and
53:   plugin operations that implement it.
54:2. **Rule enforcement** — boundary rules compile into the capability grants,
55:   budgets and network policy that are enforced on every call, with a clear
56:   refusal (and the exact missing capability) when a request is out of bounds.
57:3. **Policy** — authoring, versioning and evaluating the rules: what each
58:   identity may do, which actions need human approval (two approvals for root),
59:   and what happens to data (e.g. PII redaction, retention).
60:4. **Drop-in consumer app** — the existing UI generator repurposed: one spec
61:   renders on the web and in tools people already use, starting with **team chat** — an open-source
62:   Matrix client (Element) first, reaching other chat tools through Matrix
63:   bridges — and every action is governed by 1–3. Spec:
64:   [docs/DROP-IN-SPEC.md](docs/DROP-IN-SPEC.md).
65:   A user asks in team chat; the request is routed, checked against policy,
66:   executed through the identity or refused, and the receipt comes back in the
67:   thread.
68:
69:The web UI is optional, only if time allows.
70:
71:**Golden path** (a working product, end to end, three times in a row before
72:anything else): a user asks the agent in team chat to do something for a business
73:→ compliance routing maps it to the required controls and operations →
74:policy is evaluated → allowed operations run through the identity and return
75:receipts; a disallowed one is refused with the reason → the thread shows the
76:result, the receipts, and any redaction applied.
77:
78:Out of the critical path: the avatar/embodiment, moving identities between
79:hosts, client acquisition, and on-chain anchoring (kept only if it fits once
80:the golden path works).
81:
82:## What is new vs. what already exists
83:
84:Everything in **this repository** is developed during the hackathon. It is
85:built *on* 3tched, which already exists and is used only through its
86:published interfaces (see [docs/3TCHED-RESOURCES.md](docs/3TCHED-RESOURCES.md)).
87:
88:| New in this repo (judged) | Existing 3tched resource it uses |
89:|---|---|
90:| OSCAL catalog of 3tched capabilities, tag taxonomy, profiles, component definitions | `oscal_subid_registry` (subid discovery), `schema_tag_registry` (tag metadata, owner-scoped policy) |
91:| Compliance router: request / profile → controls → plugin operations | sealed plugin catalog, identity operation files (3tchedFS) |
92:| Rule enforcement: OSCAL rules → capability grants, budgets, OpenFlow policy; refusals with reasons | bridge per-call capability check, `openflow` / `ovsdb_bridge`, router budgets |
93:| Policy engine and policy documents (approvals, redaction, retention) | `schema_tag_registry` policies, `routing_decision`, `elevation` |
94:| Drop-in consumer app: team chat first (Matrix/Element) | chat path to Meta's model, identity receipts |
95:| Business declarations (starting with a Florida LLC) | — |
96:
97:Pre-existing and **not** part of the judged work: the identity container and
98:sled, kernel-peer admission, 3tchedFS, the bridge and MutationEngine, receipts,
99:the router, and the 3tched.com UI.
100:
101:## Architecture at a glance
102:
103:```
104:          internet only                      local filesystem only
105:  Meta model API  ◄──┐                 ┌──► 3tchedFS mount (lungs) ──► 3tched bridge
106:  blockchain      ◄──┤   IDENTITY      │      kernel-peer identity, capability check,
107:                     └── CONTAINER  ───┘      MutationEngine commit, receipt
108:                          (the twin)
109:                               │
110:            OSCAL profile ─► tag router ─► plugin operations (incus, openflow, …)
111:                               │
112:                  receipts ─► Web3 index ─► Merkle root anchored on-chain
113:```
114:
115:- The identity has **no network path to 3tched**; it reaches 3tched only
116:  through its own FUSE mount, where every operation is a typed file.
117:- Its only network is the internet: the Meta model API and the blockchain.
118:- Subsidiaries map to Linux users; the root is the 3tched control plane.
119:  See [docs/SUBSIDIARY-SLED.md](docs/SUBSIDIARY-SLED.md).
120:- The hackathon clone is `etched::hackathon`. It is stopped and not a sled
121:  identity yet. What to do next, and what is new, old, or changed:
122:  [docs/ETCHED-HACKATHON.md](docs/ETCHED-HACKATHON.md).
123:- How this compares to SPIFFE, BeyondCorp and DIDs, and what it adds:
124:  [docs/PRIOR-ART.md](docs/PRIOR-ART.md).
125:
126:## Repository layout
127:
128:| Path | Contents |
129:|---|---|
130:| `schema/` | JSON Schemas: Web3 index entry, business declarations |
131:| `oscal/` | OSCAL catalog, profiles, component definitions (Compliance Trestle workspace) |
132:| `routing/` | tag router: profile → components → operations |
133:| `enforcement/` | boundary compiler: OSCAL rules → grants, budgets, OpenFlow policy |
134:| `consumer/` | drop-in consumer apps (team chat first) |
135:| `cms/` | the CMS and its control behaviours (background) |
136:| `web3/` | index log, Merkle anchoring |
137:| `ui/` | Svelte components for the 3tched.com app |
138:| `START-HERE.md`, `CONTEXT.md` | open in omp; CONTEXT.md bundles every doc (rebuild with `tools/build-context.sh`) |
139:| `docs/` | 3tched resources, subsidiary/sled model, prior art and positioning, how to win |
140:| `SPARK-BRIEF.md` | current state, rules, open issues, progress log |
141:
142:## Working rules
143:
144:- Read `SPARK-BRIEF.md` before starting; log progress at its end (dated).
145:- Mark claims as **proven** (demonstrated, with evidence) or **planned**.
146:- Schemas here are drafts; promoted ones become sealed 3tched plugins (Rust).
147:- UI: Svelte/SvelteKit + json-render's Svelte renderer only.
148:- In pitches say "implements and evidences these controls", never
149:  "compliant" or "certified".

under what authority, and what actually happened* without trusting the agent

from trusting both autonomous agents and Web3.

Etched in Schema closes that gap from both sides: every on-chain artifact
points to the identity and authorised operation behind it, and every
operation points to the artifacts it produced, with the history anchored
on-chain.

## Goals — the new, judged product

The identity platform (3tched) existed before the hackathon and is used only
through its interfaces. The **new development, built and judged here**, is:

1. **Compliance routing** — a business's requirements become an OSCAL profile;
   OSCAL tags route each request and each requirement to the components and
   plugin operations that implement it.
2. **Rule enforcement** — boundary rules compile into the capability grants,
   budgets and network policy that are enforced on every call, with a clear
   refusal (and the exact missing capability) when a request is out of bounds.
3. **Policy** — authoring, versioning and evaluating the rules: what each
   identity may do, which actions need human approval (two approvals for root),
   and what happens to data (e.g. PII redaction, retention).
4. **Drop-in consumer app** — the existing UI generator repurposed: one spec
   renders on the web and in tools people already use, starting with **team chat** — an open-source
   Matrix client (Element) first, reaching other chat tools through Matrix
   bridges — and every action is governed by 1–3. Spec:
   [docs/DROP-IN-SPEC.md](docs/DROP-IN-SPEC.md).
   A user asks in team chat; the request is routed, checked against policy,
   executed through the identity or refused, and the receipt comes back in the
   thread.

The web UI is optional, only if time allows.

**Golden path** (a working product, end to end, three times in a row before
anything else): a user asks the agent in team chat to do something for a business
→ compliance routing maps it to the required controls and operations →
policy is evaluated → allowed operations run through the identity and return
receipts; a disallowed one is refused with the reason → the thread shows the
result, the receipts, and any redaction applied.

Out of the critical path: the avatar/embodiment, moving identities between
hosts, client acquisition, and on-chain anchoring (kept only if it fits once
the golden path works).

## What is new vs. what already exists

Everything in **this repository** is developed during the hackathon. It is
built *on* 3tched, which already exists and is used only through its
published interfaces (see [docs/3TCHED-RESOURCES.md](docs/3TCHED-RESOURCES.md)).

| New in this repo (judged) | Existing 3tched resource it uses |
|---|---|
| OSCAL catalog of 3tched capabilities, tag taxonomy, profiles, component definitions | `oscal_subid_registry` (subid discovery), `schema_tag_registry` (tag metadata, owner-scoped policy) |
| Compliance router: request / profile → controls → plugin operations | sealed plugin catalog, identity operation files (3tchedFS) |
| Rule enforcement: OSCAL rules → capability grants, budgets, OpenFlow policy; refusals with reasons | bridge per-call capability check, `openflow` / `ovsdb_bridge`, router budgets |
| Policy engine and policy documents (approvals, redaction, retention) | `schema_tag_registry` policies, `routing_decision`, `elevation` |
| Drop-in consumer app: team chat first (Matrix/Element) | chat path to Meta's model, identity receipts |
| Business declarations (starting with a Florida LLC) | — |

Pre-existing and **not** part of the judged work: the identity container and
sled, kernel-peer admission, 3tchedFS, the bridge and MutationEngine, receipts,
the router, and the 3tched.com UI.

## Architecture at a glance

```
          internet only                      local filesystem only
  Meta model API  ◄──┐                 ┌──► 3tchedFS mount (lungs) ──► 3tched bridge
  blockchain      ◄──┤   IDENTITY      │      kernel-peer identity, capability check,
                     └── CONTAINER  ───┘      MutationEngine commit, receipt
                          (the twin)
                               │
            OSCAL profile ─► tag router ─► plugin operations (incus, openflow, …)
                               │
                  receipts ─► Web3 index ─► Merkle root anchored on-chain
```

- The identity has **no network path to 3tched**; it reaches 3tched only
  through its own FUSE mount, where every operation is a typed file.
- Its only network is the internet: the Meta model API and the blockchain.
- Subsidiaries map to Linux users; the root is the 3tched control plane.
  See [docs/SUBSIDIARY-SLED.md](docs/SUBSIDIARY-SLED.md).
- The hackathon clone is `etched::hackathon`. It is stopped and not a sled
  identity yet. What to do next, and what is new, old, or changed:
  [docs/ETCHED-HACKATHON.md](docs/ETCHED-HACKATHON.md).
- How this compares to SPIFFE, BeyondCorp and DIDs, and what it adds:
  [docs/PRIOR-ART.md](docs/PRIOR-ART.md).

## Repository layout

| Path | Contents |
|---|---|
| `schema/` | JSON Schemas: Web3 index entry, business declarations |
| `oscal/` | OSCAL catalog, profiles, component definitions (Compliance Trestle workspace) |
| `routing/` | tag router: profile → components → operations |
| `enforcement/` | boundary compiler: OSCAL rules → grants, budgets, OpenFlow policy |
| `consumer/` | drop-in consumer apps (team chat first) |
| `cms/` | the CMS and its control behaviours (background) |
| `web3/` | index log, Merkle anchoring |
| `ui/` | Svelte components for the 3tched.com app |
| `START-HERE.md`, `CONTEXT.md` | open in omp; CONTEXT.md bundles every doc (rebuild with `tools/build-context.sh`) |
| `docs/` | 3tched resources, subsidiary/sled model, prior art and positioning, how to win |
| `SPARK-BRIEF.md` | current state, rules, open issues, progress log |

## Working rules

- Read `SPARK-BRIEF.md` before starting; log progress at its end (dated).
- Mark claims as **proven** (demonstrated, with evidence) or **planned**.
- Schemas here are drafts; promoted ones become sealed 3tched plugins (Rust).
- UI: Svelte/SvelteKit + json-render's Svelte renderer only.
- In pitches say "implements and evidences these controls", never
  "compliant" or "certified".

`/etc/sv/subsidiary-hackathon-3tchedfs`. Run product services as `3tched`
(`chpst -u 3tched`).

## Network rules

- The **only** service ingress on this host is `<door-ip>:8090`. The product
  must not open new listening ports to the outside.
- The team-chat adapter connects **outbound** to its homeserver (no inbound
  webhook). A local homeserver for the demo binds to loopback only.
- The identity container (`3tchedCtlChatbot`) has internet-only egress
  (bridge `hackbr0`, ACL `internet-only`) and no network path to 3tched; it
  reaches 3tched only through its mount (**proven**).
- Any network change must be recorded in
  `/srv/git/odbus-verified/docs/src/operations/network.md`.

## Models

- **Meta (required for the product's AI steps)**: Meta's Model API,
  `https://api.meta.ai/v1` (OpenAI-style `/chat/completions`), model
  `muse-spark-1.3` (**proven**, 2026-10-28). Credentials: `META_API_KEY`,
  `META_MODEL`, `META_MODEL_BASE_URL` — in `~/.bash_secrets` for `jeremy`
  (development) and in `/home/3tched/.config/etched/env` (owner `3tched`,
  mode 0600) for the running service. The model reasons before answering:
  give it a generous `max_tokens` (800+).
- **TypeSafe Jev** (judgments): `TYPESAFE_API_KEY` in `~/.bash_secrets` (user
  `jeremy`); see `review/jev_strategy.py` for the request format.
- 3tched's chat router (`127.0.0.1:8084`) currently uses a Qwen model; do not
  depend on it for the judged product.

## Team chat (planned)

- Matrix first; demo client Element. A homeserver is needed: a lightweight
  one (e.g. a Rust homeserver such as Conduit/conduwuit) on loopback, or an
  existing account on a public homeserver.
- Adapter: a Matrix bot (e.g. `matrix-rust-sdk`), outbound only, run as
  `3tched` under runit.

## Language choices

- Router, policy, enforcement, chat adapter: **Rust** preferred (matches
  3tched; `cargo` as `jeremy`, run the binary as `3tched`). TypeScript is
  acceptable where the UI generator's renderer code is reused.
- UI renderer for the web: Svelte + json-render (existing).
- OSCAL: `trestle` (as `jeremy`).

## Secrets

Never commit keys. Put runtime secrets in a root- or `3tched`-owned file with
mode `0600` (e.g. `/home/3tched/.config/etched/env`) and load them in the
runit `run` script.

## Logs and receipts

- Service logs: `/var/log/<service>/current` (svlogd).
- The subsidiary mount's log: `/var/log/op-dbus/subsidiary-hackathon-3tchedfs/`.
- Receipts are the evidence: keep `operation_id` and `event_hash` for every
  action the product takes, and show them to the user.

# Dev cycle: blob → mount → identity

**The method is the blob.** In 3tched a plugin *is* its schema, sealed into a
blob; a method exists if and only if its blob is in the sealed catalog. The
identity (the chatbot / the subsidiary) never calls code directly: it sees the
sealed methods as typed files in its own 3tchedFS mount, calls them there, and
every call is admitted, checked and receipted by the platform. Every new
method built for the hackathon follows this path — that is the dev cycle.

```text
 this repo (new logic)        platform registration        sealed catalog
 ┌───────────────────┐       ┌────────────────────┐       ┌──────────────────────────┐
 │ crate: types,     │──────▶│ plugin schema +    │──────▶│ <plugin>.<hash16>.blob   │
 │ rules, tests      │       │ dispatch (op-dbus) │ seal  │ (/dev/shm/opdbus/...)    │
 └───────────────────┘       └────────────────────┘       └────────────┬─────────────┘
                                                                        │ projected by 3tchedFS
                                                                        ▼
 receipt ◀── bridge: kernel/credential identity, ◀── call file ◀── identity's mount
 (operation id,      exact capability, commit          (write args,   operations/<plugin>/<method>/call
  chain event)                                          read result)
```

## The three relationships

| Relationship | What it means | Where to see it |
|---|---|---|
| **blob ↔ method** | A method exists only as a sealed blob; its schema is the single source of its arguments, results and required capability | `ls /dev/shm/opdbus/plugin-blobs/` (72 blobs today); `opblob inspect <file.blob>` |
| **blob ↔ mount** | 3tchedFS projects each sealed method as `operations/<plugin>/<method>/{call,metadata.json,input.schema.json,output.schema.json}`; a new blob appears in every identity's mount, with no mount change | `/home/3tched/Hackathon/3tchedfs/operations/` (as `3tched`) |
| **mount ↔ chatbot** | The identity acts **only** through its mount, by writing to call files. There is no MCP path: MCP was removed and replaced by 3tchedFS. `3tched-fs toolsets --publish` only announces the sealed method list on EMQX; it does not call anything | call-file helper `3tched-callfile` |

## The UI is in the same cycle

The UI is **derived from the blobs**, never written against a separate API:

| Step | What happens |
|---|---|
| Screens | Rendered from a plugin's **sealed schema** (`schema_renderer.render_schema`) — a new method's blob gives it a form and result view automatically |
| Components | Only components declared in the catalog sealed in the `json_render` blob; a generated spec is **validated against that catalog** before it is shown |
| Actions | Call the **same sealed method** for whoever is acting: a human through the door (the one generic `PluginService/CallMethod`, with their own credential); the identity through its mount's call file. Same blob, same capability check, same receipt |
| Results | Every action shows its **receipt** (operation id, outcome, capability) — and a refusal shows the missing capability |

So a new method needs no UI code to appear: seal the blob, and the UI can
render and call it. Hand-written UI is only for composition and the
governance components (receipt, refusal, approval request, redaction notice).
No MCP anywhere in the UI path.

## Each plugin is a schema feed

A sealed plugin is not only callable — it **publishes itself**. Subscribers
(the UI, the identity) receive one stream per plugin over the bridge's
`Subscribe`:

| Frame | Carries |
|---|---|
| schema frame (`SCHEMA_MIGRATION`) | the plugin's sealed schema and its schema hash, so a consumer can render forms and validate before calling |
| state frames | committed values per object path, each with a **generation** number (older generations are ignored) and the catalog hash |
| tombstones | deletions, so a removed object never reappears from an older frame |
| withheld | private state the subscriber is not entitled to stays withheld (`withheld-or-unavailable`) |

The UI keeps feed data under `/plugins` and `/pluginFeeds` **read-only**: a
UI can never write state into a feed; only a sealed method call changes it.

## How state is read

State has one writer: **MutationEngine**, which commits the result of each
admitted call and only then notifies subscribers. Readers never see an
uncommitted value.

| Reader | How |
|---|---|
| Live consumers (UI, identity) | the plugin's **schema feed** (above) — values derived from committed state, never from a request payload |
| Point-in-time | committed state in shared memory, `/dev/shm/opdbus/state/<plugin>.json` (root-only; e.g. `incus`, `identity_sled`, `chat_router`, `cron`, `json_render`) |
| Through the mount | the plugin's read operations (`operations/<plugin>/<read-method>/call`). The mount's `plugins/<id>/value.json` files are meant for this but currently return EIO — use read operations |

## How state is archived

Nothing is overwritten without a record; history is kept in layers:

| Layer | Where | What it holds |
|---|---|---|
| Receipts / chain | MutationEngine chain events (`operation_id`, `event_id`, `event_hash`, hash-linked) | who did what, under which capability, with which outcome |
| Snowball | `/var/lib/opdbus/snowball/{timing,vectors,state,snapshots}` — Btrfs subvolumes | a streaming audit trail of plugin footprints, automatic read-only snapshots with rolling retention, replicable with btrfs send/receive |
| Vectors | Qdrant `snowball_footprints` (~10k entries) | the archived footprints embedded for semantic search ("what changed in X last week?") |
| Sealed catalog | `/var/lib/opdbus/plugin-blobs` (persisted copy of the live catalog) | which methods existed, by blob hash |

For the hackathon this is what makes "every action is attributable" checkable:
a receipt in the UI points at a chain event, the snowball keeps the state it
produced, and the Web3 index can anchor the chain head.

## Steps for a new method (e.g. `approvals.request_approval`)

1. **Logic, in this repo.** Types, rules and tests in a crate here (e.g.
   `approvals/`). No I/O. This is the judged, new work.
2. **Register as a plugin, on the platform.** A thin schema + dispatch module in
   `/srv/git/odbus-verified/crates/op-plugins/src/state_plugins/<name>.rs`,
   registered in `default_registry.rs`, calling this repo's crate. Follow that
   repo's `AGENTS.md` (plugin is the schema; no parallel schema files). Keep it
   an adapter: decisions stay in this repo's crate.
3. **Seal a development catalog, without touching live.** Build, then
   `opblob seal-plugins <dev-catalog-dir>` and inspect the new blob
   (`opblob inspect`). The live catalog is unchanged.
4. **Release.** The only deploy path is the platform release
   (`./activate-golden.sh` → slot activation). After it, the blob is in the live
   catalog and the operation file appears in the subsidiary's mount
   automatically.
5. **Grant.** The identity gets the method's exact capability (an owner-approved
   grant change). Without it, the call is refused with the capability named —
   which is itself demonstrable.
6. **Call and verify.** As the identity: write arguments to the call file,
   read the result from the same handle, keep the `operation_id` and
   `event_hash` as evidence.

## Mounts today (2026-10-28)

| Mount | Identity | Status |
|---|---|---|
| `/home/3tched/Hackathon/3tchedfs` (host) | Still the root chatbot session `b0c777e3-0955-cd8b-3d01-ca12998cae28`. The clone `etched::hackathon` is not admitted yet. | mounted, runit `subsidiary-hackathon-3tchedfs` |
| `/run/mount/3tchedfs`, `/run/mount/threetched` (inside the identity container) | same identity | mounted |
| `/run/mounts/3tchedFS`, `/run/mounts/threetched` (host) | owner `<owner-session>` | **not mounted** — fstab entries missing since the reboot; owner's decision to restore |

Known limits: live state reads (`plugins/*/value.json`) return EIO — use
operations; the `3tched-fs call --mount` CLI cannot drive guest-kernel mounts —
use the call files directly. Do not use the leftover `3tched-fs mcp`
subcommand or the bridge's `/mcp` endpoint: MCP is retired in favour of the
mount.

Here's the exact gap — and the fast path you're asking for:

**Why you keep hearing "not built / not sealed / not deployed":**
- `hackathon/org-chart`, `catalog-routing`, `approvals/` exist and pass as pure libs, but none are registered in `crates/op-plugins/src/default_registry.rs` → so no blob → no mount file → no receipt → nothing to see.
- `target/release/opblob` exists from an older build, but not from these crates.

**What I would do, in your order — develop → build → deploy, verify after:**

1. **Develop (1 edit):** add thin adapter `crates/op-plugins/src/state_plugins/<name>.rs` + 1 line in `default_registry.rs` per crate. Logic stays in `hackathon/`; adapter only maps schema + dispatch. No parallel schema files.
2. **Build:** `CXXFLAGS="-include cstdint" cargo build --workspace --release` from repo root. One cargo at a time.
3. **Seal (prep, not live):** `sudo target/release/opblob seal-shm` + `persist`. Then `build-golden.sh` to stage golden.

# Etched in Schema — brief for Muse Spark

Hackathon: Meta Model API, **Startup Track — judged on a working product**.
Builder: Jeremy Hobson (3tched).

**Scope (owner, 2026-10-28):** the identity/3tched platform predates the
hackathon and is used through its interfaces. The new, judged development is
(1) compliance routing, (2) rule enforcement, (3) policy, and (4) a drop-in
consumer app (team chat first). The UI is optional. See README "Goals" for the
golden path. Sections below about the avatar, CMS demo and on-chain anchoring
are background, not the critical path.
State as of 2026-10-28. Everything marked **proven** was demonstrated on the
host that day; everything else is planned.

## The project in one paragraph

A self-contained 3tched identity — the "twin", the living embodiment of a
3tched subsidiary — turns a business goal into deployed, verified
infrastructure. It acts only through its own typed filesystem (3tchedFS),
every action is authorised against its capabilities and leaves a
tamper-evident receipt, and a Web3 index anchored on-chain lets anyone verify
who did what, under what authority, without trusting the agent or operator.
That link between on-chain artifacts and accountable, authorised actors is the
gap blocking Web3 adoption.

## Proven today

- **Identity container**: `3tchedCtlChatbot` (Incus, pool `3tched`, profile
  `3tched-lungs`), identity session `<subsidiary-session>`,
  service principal, persist volume, kept running by runit `chatbot-identity`.
- **First-person operation call**: inside the container, write the plain JSON
  arguments to `/run/mount/3tchedfs/operations/<plugin>/<method>/call` (open
  read-write, write, fsync, read back on the same handle). Example
  `identity_sled/get_own_identity` with `{}` returned the identity, operation
  `51c8f91c-c2f1-4688-a985-fb41684adfff`, chain events 10389/10390, outcome
  completed. The bridge identifies the caller from the kernel peer over the
  lungs Unix socket, checks the exact capability, commits via MutationEngine.
- **Infrastructure operations available to the identity**: `incus/*`
  (create/start/stop/snapshot/devices), `ovsdb_bridge/*` (bridges, ports,
  transact), plus ~70 plugins. Each call is checked against the identity's
  grants.
- **No network path to 3tched**: the twin talks to 3tched only through its FUSE
  mount. Its only network will be the internet (Meta API, blockchain).
- **Chat path**: UI (`http://<door-ip>:8080`) → door `<door-ip>:8090` →
  `chat_router.Chat` → zeroclaw router on `127.0.0.1:8084` (protocol
  `zeroclaw.v1`) → model. Every turn receipted.
- **Avatar**: `IdentityAvatar.svelte` speaks a fixed intro script (exact
  wording, no model) and answers spoken or typed questions via the chat path.

## Where things are

| Thing | Path |
|---|---|
| Backend (Rust workspace) | `/srv/git/odbus-verified` — read its `AGENTS.md` and `HANDOFF.md` first |
| UI (SvelteKit + json-render) | `/srv/git/3tched.com` (has uncommitted WIP — do not publish it as-is) |
| UI build actually live | scratch worktree of 3tched.com HEAD + `tched_router`→`chat_router` + avatar |
| This repo | `/srv/git/etched-in-schema` — Web3 index schema, LLC declaration schema |
| Recovered execution tracker | branch `recover/execution-tracker`, worktree `/srv/git/odbus-tracker-recover` (compiles; not deployed) |
| Router config | `/var/lib/tched-router/config.toml` (root; backups `*.bak-20261028-*`) |
| Qdrant | `127.0.0.1:6333` — `repos_specs_docs_voyage_4_lite`, `repos_repomix_voyage_context_4`, `snowball_footprints`, `blockchain_footprints` |

## Rules that must not be broken

- The plugin IS the schema. Backend schemas live only in Rust plugins under
  `crates/op-plugins/src/state_plugins/`, sealed into blobs. No standalone
  schema files in op-dbus (that is why drafts live in this repo).
- UI is Svelte/SvelteKit + Vite + json-render's Svelte renderer only. Every
  visible element is a catalog component.
- Never edit Cozo directly, never bypass a permission denial, never add or
  remove Btrfs members outside explicit identity provisioning.
- Deployment is `./activate-golden.sh` / `op-release-launch release`
  (btrfs send/receive slots). Never hand-copy binaries onto the host as a deploy.
- One Cargo process at a time; release builds need `CXXFLAGS="-include cstdint"`.
- Tests only when the owner asks.
- Commit and push at the end of every working turn (owner policy, 2026-10-28): public repo `github.com/repr0bated/etched-in-schema`, branch `master`. No turn ends with unpushed work.

## Plan (10 days)

1. OSCAL catalog of 3tched capabilities with a tag taxonomy; component
   definitions for 3–5 plugins (Compliance Trestle is installed: `trestle`).
2. Tag routing: profile → components → plugin operations.
3. Boundary rules compiled into capability grants and budgets (the bridge
   already enforces grants on every call).

# How to win this hackathon

Ten priorities for the demo and submission. When in doubt, choose whatever
makes the golden path more reliable or more verifiable.

1. **Unforgettable first 30 seconds.** The avatar speaks the exact intro
   script, then immediately does one real thing, with its receipt appearing on
   screen. Show proof before explaining anything.

2. **Let a judge verify something themselves.** Hand them a receipt ID or
   on-chain anchor and a one-step way to check it (link or QR code). "Don't
   trust me, check it" is the thesis made physical.

3. **Show one refusal live.** Ask the identity to do something outside its
   OSCAL boundary; the bridge refuses with the exact missing capability. An
   agent that *can't* misbehave beats one that doesn't.

4. **Use Meta's model visibly and well.** Show Muse Spark doing the reasoning
   (planning the business, mapping requirements to controls), say so on
   screen, and let it make one real tool call through the identity's mount.

5. **Protect the golden path above everything.** Intro → "create a CMS for this
   business" → provision → receipts → anchor. Run it end to end daily from
   Day 5. If it does not pass three times in a row, add nothing new.

6. **Redaction is the "wow" moment.** Content with a name, email and phone
   number is published and masked automatically, with the receipt naming the
   policy. Everyone understands it instantly.

7. **A fallback for every live dependency.** Record a full run and know the
   exact step at which you would switch to it. Model, chain or Wi-Fi can fail
   on stage; a calm switch still scores.

8. **Tell a story with a real business.** One believable small business (e.g.
   a Fort Lauderdale firm that needs a compliant client portal), with a name
   and a problem, solved by the identity.

9. **Say the positioning line out loud.** *"Workload identity like SPIFFE
   proves who is calling. Etched in Schema also proves what it was allowed to
   do — and what it actually did."*

10. **Ship the evidence, not just the demo.** Public repo with a README that
    separates new from pre-existing work, a short video, a one-page
    architecture diagram, and a live link judges can open later.

**Bonus: freeze scope on Day 7.** After that, only polish, rehearse and fix.

content.text:
That's exactly how to frame it for judges — skeleton allowed, product new.

**How it's defined here — and in your submission:**

Allowed skeleton = anything that existed before 10-28 and you only use through its interface. You don't claim it:
- identity container, 3tchedFS mount, bridge/MutationEngine, receipts, `chat_router`, router on 8084, 3tched.com UI

New cycle / new product = what you built 10-28 → now, judged:
1. compliance routing — OSCAL catalog + tag taxonomy + profile → operations
2. rule enforcement — rules → grants/budgets/OpenFlow policy, refusals name the missing cap
3. policy — `approvals/` 2-human root, redaction, retention
4. drop-in consumer — team chat first, every action receipted

Whole project reinvented itself because the loop is new: business goal → routed → policy-checked → executed through the mount → receipt → Web3 anchor. The platform is the engine, Etched is the new car around it.

**Say it in one line:**
> "Built *on* 3tched, which predates the hackathon and is used only via its mount/blob interfaces. All routing, enforcement, policy, and consumer code in `hackathon/` is new 10-28 to 10-30 — see `spark-provenance-20261029` → `4d051ed` and the merge `4d815ca` preserving all 58 SHAs."

That plus WINNING #10 — README separating new from pre-existing + receipts + video — is what makes "new product" stick.

content.text:
Yes — appliance is the right pitch, with one word-swap to keep you safe.

**Call it this:**
> Governed identity appliance — locks receipts to ETH, not just our hash chain.

Why that wording:
- Existing code has hash-linked `ChainEvent` + Merkle `GetProof` (`op-state-store/event_chain.rs`, `operation.proto`) — that's tamper-evident receipts, **not a blockchain**. Don't call that blockchain or judges will ding you.
- ETH anchoring is 100% new: only `hackathon/web3/` + `schema/index-entry.schema.json`, default Base Sepolia + EAS. Zero ETH in `crates/`. That's your "totally new everywhere."
- Avoid `compliance appliance` as the noun — repo rule is never say "compliant/certified", say "implements and evidences controls." `Compliance-routing appliance` keeps the SEO without the cert claim.

**Demo line:**
> "SPIFFE proves who called. This appliance also proves what it was allowed to do — and anchors what it did to Base Sepolia so you can check without trusting me."

Keep anchoring as planned-until-golden-path-passes-3x, then it becomes the closer, not the dependency.

#!/bin/sh
# release-bridge.sh — one-command bridge release, in the only safe order:
# pull -> checkout -> build -> seal -> activate (snapshot/send-receive/rotate).
#
#   sudo ./release-bridge.sh
#
# Overrides: REPO=/srv/git/odbus-verified BRANCH=rewrite-fresh-bridge
#
# Order matters and is not negotiable:
# - cargo build never reads SHM, so build first.
# - opblob seal-shm/persist writes the catalog the new bridge will consume.
# - activate-golden.sh prepares golden, sends/receives into the inactive
#   slot, rotates, and keeps active+previous (previous = rollback).
# The bridge is never started before the seal, and binaries are never
# hand-copied onto the running host.
set -eu
PATH=/usr/sbin:/usr/bin:/sbin:/bin
export PATH

[ "$(id -u)" = 0 ] || { echo "release-bridge: run as root: sudo $0" >&2; exit 1; }
OWNER=${SUDO_USER:-jeremy}
BRANCH=${BRANCH:-rewrite-fresh-bridge}

# --- locate the repo -------------------------------------------------------
REPO=${REPO:-}
if [ -z "$REPO" ]; then
    for candidate in /srv/git/odbus-verified /home/$OWNER/odbus-verified /home/$OWNER/odbus-combined; do
        if [ -d "$candidate/.git" ] || [ -f "$candidate/.git" ]; then REPO=$candidate; break; fi
    done
fi
[ -n "$REPO" ] && [ -d "$REPO" ] || { echo "release-bridge: repo not found; set REPO=<path>" >&2; exit 1; }
echo "release-bridge: repo=$REPO branch=$BRANCH owner=$OWNER"

as_owner() {
    # Run a command as the repo owner (root-owned git in a user repo trips
    # safe.directory and creates root-owned build artifacts).
    runuser -u "$OWNER" -- env HOME="/home/$OWNER" \
        PATH="/home/$OWNER/.cargo/bin:/usr/local/bin:/usr/bin:/bin" "$@"
}

# --- 1. pull + checkout ----------------------------------------------------
echo "== fetch =="
as_owner git -C "$REPO" fetch origin --prune

  A[chat-catalog.ts: tchedRouterPicker] --> B[chat-registry.ts -> tchedRouterPicker.svelte]
  B --> C[ModelPicker.svelte]

```

displayContent.text:
# Tag taxonomy v1 (draft)

Tags route requests: profile → controls → plugin operations. One tag per
control in `catalogs/etched-catalog/catalog.json`, stored as OSCAL props
(`ns: https://3tched.com/ns/oscal`, `name: tag`). Mirrors live in 3tched's
`schema_tag_registry` (tag semantics + owner-scoped policies); this file is
the draft, the registry is authoritative at runtime.

| Tag | Control | Sealed operations (candidate) | Evidence |
|---|---|---|---|
| `pii` | `etched-pt-1` | `schema_tag_registry/get_policy` | redaction receipt naming policy |
| `audit` | `etched-au-1` | `identity_sled/get_own_identity`, `routing_decision/get_decision`, `routing_decision/list_decisions` | operation receipt (`operation_id`, `event_hash`) |
| `access-control` | `etched-ac-1` | `elevation/authorize_task`, `schema_tag_registry/get_tag` | refusal receipt (missing capability + rule); approval record |
| `retention` | `etched-si-1` | `cron/create_job`, `workflows/start_workflow` | scheduled-operation receipt |
| `integrity` | `etched-in-1` | `identity_sled/get_identity`; anchor needs a sealed `web3` method (none yet — drafts only) | anchor record (index entry + tx) |

Qualifier tags (planned, for the router data model in `routing/DATA-MODEL.md`):
`data:private` / `data:public`, `action:read` / `action:write` /
`action:publish`, `approval:root` (two humans), `surface:team-chat` /
`surface:web`.

Rules:
- Every request carries ≥1 control tag; the router resolves tags → controls → operations.
- Tags never grant authority; grants come from the compiled profile (enforcement). A tag miss is a refusal, not a default-allow.
- New tags are added here first, then registered in `schema_tag_registry`.

content.text:
Found the real shape of it — and one thing I'm not touching without your explicit word:

**Submit exists.** It's labeled `Apply model` (`ModelPicker.svelte:59`, `runtime.applyRoute`). If you see no submit, it's because the catalog came back empty so Apply renders disabled — data missing, not code missing. Same for Refresh: the button is wired (`refreshProviders` → `model_registry refresh` + `list_providers/list_models`); failures surface as the `catalogError` line, not silence.

**Elevate stays until you explicitly approve its removal.** `ControlPlanePicker` requires a per-task root ticket (`elevation.authorize` → `chat_router config_patch`, `router.write@v1`). Dropping that weakens a security boundary, which I'm not doing on my own. Note the self path already skips it: `setControlPlaneModel` uses `apply_own_agent_route` (`agent.route.self.write@v1`) with no elevation when access is `self`. If you're seeing `Elevate and apply model`, you're on the non-self path — that's working as designed, and removing it needs a grant decision, not a UI edit.

**opencode, and your "two versions":** backend declares `opencode` (route `custom:opencode`, kind `cli`, aliases `opencode.go` + `deepseek-v4-flash-free`) with **no endpoint/auth in defaults** — contrast `salad`, which ships `endpoint + bearer`. And every `model_route` is `status: declared, available: false` ("backend availability must be projected before execution"). So both routes — opencode and the custom loopback — project as unavailable, which is exactly the dead picker you're seeing. `oc-authorization` is the `resolve_catalog_model_binding` uri/oauth binding; with no `inference_url_prefix` it stays unconfirmed.

Tell me which two you meant — the two aliases (`opencode.go` vs `deepseek-v4-flash-free`) or the two providers (opencode + custom) — plus the picker's state line, and I'll trace that one call.

content: So when this is in the blob and it's defined as a surface, it's not yet a approved c- uh catalog component, right? So what is it called at this stage

content.thinking: Clarifying the lifecycle stages and naming for a taxonomy picker spec before it becomes an approved catalog component.

content.text:
Right — not approved yet. At this stage it's a **candidate** (a *suggestion*: `suggestion_id` + `spec_hash`, previewable but not live).

The lifecycle in `ui-gallery.ts` terms:

1. **Candidate** — `suggestCandidate`: spec exists, shows in "Submitted canvas preview," nothing published.
2. **Promoted catalog entry** — `promoteCandidate` (requires the reviewed `suggestion_id` to match): now in the **active catalog**, renderable by type name like `tchedRouterPicker`.
3. **Retired** — `retireCatalogEntry` (elevated): removed from the active catalog, drafts stay usable.

So "approved catalog component" = promoted + active. Our taxonomy picker would enter at step 1 as a candidate spec built only from already-catalogued table components — previewable immediately, promotable through review, and until then the dashboard can't address it by type.

content: Release. That is available and it's stored into whatever, where would it be stored for them? We have our blobs and our schema, where is it stored normally

content.thinking:
Describing normal storage locations for sealed blobs, catalog, and specs across SHM and persisted paths per docs.

Pinpointing promoted catalog entries to plugin state and releases to btrfs snapshots.

content.text:
Three different stores, depending on which "it" you mean:

| What | Where it lives normally |
|---|---|
| Sealed schemas (the blob IS the plugin) | Live: `/dev/shm/opdbus/plugin-blobs/<plugin>.<hash16>.blob` (72 today) · persisted across reboot: `/var/lib/opdbus/plugin-blobs` |
| Committed state — including promoted gallery/catalog entries | `/dev/shm/opdbus/state/<plugin>.json` (root-only; `json_render` among them) — single writer MutationEngine, then history into `/var/lib/opdbus/snowball/{timing,vectors,state,snapshots}` + Qdrant `snowball_footprints` |
| A whole release | `/opt/op-dbus/releases/<id>`, selected by the `/opt/op-dbus/current` symlink (active + previous kept for rollback); dashboard static under `/usr/local/share/op-dbus/dashboard/` |

So our taxonomy picker, once promoted, lands as a `json_render` catalog entry in that plugin's committed state — readable live from SHM, archived by snowball, shipped inside the release snapshot. The candidate spec itself is just JSON until promotion; nothing persists it until then.

content: I'm trying just to get the concept of the whole how it is introduced in to a system that doesn't have blobs. Hmph

content.thinking: Explaining the bootstrap process for introducing the first content-addressed sealed blob via the sole writer sealer and genesis flow.

content.text:
The cold-start story, end to end:

1. **No blobs, just code.** Plugins are registered in `default_registry.rs` — schema + dispatch, plain Rust. Nothing runs yet.
2. **One writer makes the first blob.** `opblob` (the sole sealer) reads each registered schema, validates it, hashes it, and writes `<plugin>.<hash16>.blob` into a catalog directory. The hash *is* the identity — a blob exists ⟺ its bytes hash to its name.
3. **That directory becomes the catalog.** Sealed into the release snapshot, shipped by send/receive, activated under `/opt/op-dbus/current`. The bridge never creates blobs; on startup it only *consumes* the catalog read-only and projects each blob as mount files (`operations/<plugin>/<method>/call`).
4. **Trust without prior blobs** comes from build provenance, not from the blob store: pinned manifests, binary digests, and the service verifying manifest + commit + digest before exec. The first seal is reproducible from source + pins — anyone rebuilding gets identical bytes.

So "introduced" = compile the schema, hash it into a name, ship the bytes. After that the system is self-describing: every method, form, and UI component derives from bytes already in the store.

Mapping individual UI fragments to the page-level chat spec and identifying quadrant as the four-panel composition.

content.text:
That's the right split — and yes, picker is the wrong home for it. Here's the design as you described it, in the system's own terms:

**Page chat spec = the composition root.** Like `antigravitySpec`: one root `container` whose `children` are independent fragments — `chat-header`, `tched-picker`, `antigravity-chat`, and now addable siblings: `grants-console`, the quadrant set, schema view, web view. Each fragment is its own spec subtree with its own element ids. The picker stays route-only; composition happens one level up, in the page spec the chatbot owns.

**Your "quadrant" already exists as a bundle.** `compositions.rs` emits exactly it: provenance + orgchart + feed in one JSON object, plus the grants console makes four. Each is individually addressable, so the chatbot (or user) appends fragments per request instead of one monolith: barebones chat first (request → schema → render), then `+console`, `+quadrant`, `+schema` as asked.

**Memory is retained by the thread, not the fragments.** `conversation_id` / `chat-thread` (`stream_antigravity_01`) carries history; fragments are stateless renders of committed state, so adding or removing a surface never drops the conversation.

So the build order writes itself: barebones chat spec first (already the pattern), then one fragment builder at a time behind the same catalog-components rule — console, quadrant set, schema — each previewable as a candidate before promotion.

content.thinking: Explaining that new spec fragments from existing components need no recompile or reseal, while new catalogs do.

content.text:
For spec-only fragments like these: **correct — no recompile, no reseal, no release.** A spec is just JSON naming component types that are *already* sealed in the `json_render` catalog. Validate it against the catalog, render it, done. Promotion to the active catalog is a method call (`promoteCandidate`) that commits state — still no build involved.

The line where that stops being true:

- **New component *type*** (a Svelte component that doesn't exist yet) → UI repo change + rebuild dashboard assets + the `json_render` reference catalog has to admit it, which means a reseal of that blob and a release to ship it.
- **New method/capability** → full cycle: code → register → reseal blob → golden release → grant.

So: compose from what's sealed = free, instant. Extend what's sealed = reseal + release. That's exactly why the barebones-first order pays — console, quadrant, schema views are all composable today from the existing table/log/topology components.

content.text:
Understood — and with the approvals model hammered out (owner + co-signer, chatbot holds no execution grants), the per-task password button is redundant. Here's exactly what I'd change, nothing more:

**Edits (UI repo only):**
- `ControlPlanePicker.svelte` — drop the `Elevation`/`SudoPrompt` path; the button becomes plain `Apply model` calling the existing `set` without `elevate` (same shape as `ModelPicker.svelte:58`). Enforcement stays at the door: `chat_router config_patch` still requires its capability grant — identity allowed → allowed, denied → refusal naming the capability. No grant broadening, no new methods.
- `chat-catalog.ts:43` description — remove "require root password authorization," replace with "admitted by the caller's grant."
- Tests: `ModelPicker.test.ts` control-plane cases expecting `Elevate and apply model` + `SudoPrompt` → expect plain Apply; `control-plane-model.test.ts` elevate-mock cases for `config_patch` → expect direct call with capability asserted.

**What stays:** door capability checks, co-signer rule for root actions, chatbot no-execution. The identity check *is* the gate now.

Confirm and I'll make those three edits + run that test file.

content.thinking: Analyzing route binding behavior and separating picker, inference, and control plane bindings.

content.text:
Mostly yes — with one correction that matters: the carryover happens **server-side, not in the UI.**

`submit` sends only the message (plus `text` vs `application` for ui_render) — never the picker's draft. What answers is the **applied native binding** that Apply wrote (`apply_catalog_model_binding` → reference + uri). So:

- **Personal / project / notebook modes** — your applied route carries over automatically. One Apply, every turn in those modes uses it.
- **Control Plane** — separate dedicated binding (`agents.control_plane.model_provider` via `config_patch`). That's why it has its own picker section; your personal Apply doesn't move it.
- **Accountability** — same pattern, its own observed binding (`audit.observed_alias`).
- **UI render** — ignores the picker entirely; backend's configured generation model, `response_mode: application`.

So the mental model: picker Apply = set the rail, all personal turns ride it; the two governed modes have their own rails, and UI-gen runs on the house model.

content.thinking: Validating backend catalog requirements and UI rendering constraints for unknown or retired types.

content.text:
Exactly — that's the load-bearing rule, and it bites at two points:

1. **Render time:** every generated spec is validated against the sealed `json_render` catalog before anything shows. Unknown component type → no render, not a broken render.
2. **Call time:** every action goes through `CallMethod` against the sealed method table. Unsealed method, or sealed but ungranted for that identity → refusal naming the capability, surfaced verbatim.

So the order is forced: backend method/component in the sealed catalog first, *then* a functioning UI element can come out. Anything the chatbot dreams up outside the catalog is preview-only (candidate) until promotion seals it. That's why your barebones-first order works — console, quadrant, schema views compose from already-sealed table/log/topology pieces, zero catalog gap.

content.text:
Exactly — work it backwards from the UI you want:

**Subvolume manager UI needs, minimum:**
- `btrfs` list (bounded pages — thousands of rows means paged reads like `list_models`' 500-row pages, never one unbounded dump)
- `btrfs` create + delete (each its own sealed method, each its own capability)
- Receipts per action (`operation_id`/`event_hash`) in the table, refusals naming the missing grant

Which is a new taxonomy row: tag → control → the three `(btrfs, method, capability)` triples + "receipt" as evidence. And the same two gates apply: the `btrfs` methods must be sealed (the `btrfs.*` blob is in your live 72 — verify the exact method names with `opblob inspect` before speccing), and the acting identity must hold each capability or the buttons render dead with a stated reason.

That's the drill for every future element: list the verbs the UI needs, check each verb is a sealed method + granted capability, spec from catalog components, promote. No verb, no button.

One sharpening: "full control" = **every verb the element needs, inside its boundary** — not blanket admin. List + create + delete scoped to the identity's own subvolumes (same pattern as the `etched0`-only OpenFlow rule: refuse anything outside the boundary with the reason named). The bridge already enforces per-call, so the grant set *is* the control surface.

That's also what makes partial grants useful elsewhere: they're how you demo the refusal path live. But for the subvolume manager itself — yes, the acting identity holds the complete verb set or don't build the buttons.

content.thinking: Defining spec-builder boundaries to return only JSON data with no execution, relying on renderer and capability checks.

content.text:
Exactly — and that's structural, not policy. The builders are pure functions: static rows in, `serde_json::Value` out. No I/O, no network, no `Command`, no socket — the crate denies it by construction (`no I/O, no network` is in all three manifests).

So a spec can never *do* anything. It can only name catalog component types for the renderer, and the one form in the whole console (`dashboardFormPreview`) submits nothing — proposals travel the approval path. Execution happens only through `CallMethod`, one granted method at a time, receipted.

That's the boundary doing the work for you: JSON out, commands impossible. No restriction list needed because there's no channel to restrict — the return type is the whole surface.

content.text:
Three different shelves — spec, candidate, catalog member:

- **Snippets (repo, not stored in the system):** `examples/*.rs` emitters, `references/` (canvas-contract, dashboard-examples, reference-chat), pagespecs. Plain files emitting JSON to `local/*.spec.json`. This is where our taxonomy picker lives right now.
- **Gallery = staging (plugin state):** `save_candidate` stores a spec as a **candidate** (`suggestion_id` + `spec_hash`). Visible in preview, not addressable by live pages. `listCandidates` reads them back.
- **Catalog = live (same plugin state, promoted flag):** `promoteCandidate` moves a reviewed suggestion into the **active catalog** as a `CatalogEntry` — now referenceable by `type:` in any Spec. `retireCatalogEntry` pulls it back out.

So promotion is a state flip inside `json_render` (committed via MutationEngine → SHM → snowball), not a file move. Drafts live in git; candidates live in the gallery; members live in the active catalog.

content.thinking: Confirming grant flow must use the org-chart compiler as the sole authority without side-channel overrides.

content.text:
Exactly right — it can't be a side-channel grant, or the compiler stops being the sole authority. It ties in like this:

1. **Chart facts in:** the chatbot's position holds a role carrying the chat capability (same as any grant — membership + role + attributes, nothing edited directly).
2. **Compile:** `org-chart compile` → `grants_for(member)` yields the capability with provenance (`via_role`/`via_position`).
3. **`decide()` consumes it:** the request is allowed because the compiled grant covers it — same path as every other decision.
4. **Materialize to live:** the compiled output is what the live grant store must reflect — verified against the sealed catalog hash (`grants_for_verified`), never a hand-written grant row.

So the packet I sketched becomes a chart edit + recompile + verify, not a direct grant write. A manual grant that overrides the compiler would break the invariant the whole console is built on — good catch, that's the line.

142:/// authority.
143:pub(crate) fn enforce_bridge_capability_with_schema(
144:    schema: Option<&JsonValue>,
145:    plugin_id: &str,
146:    method_name: &str,
147:    capability_id: Option<&str>,
148:    identity: Option<&GhostbridgeIdentity>,
149:) -> Result<(), ProtoMutationError> {
150:    let method_capability = schema
151:        .and_then(|schema| method_capability_from_schema(schema, method_name))
152:        .ok_or_else(|| {
153:            capability_denied(
154:                plugin_id,
155:                method_name,
156:                capability_id,
157:                "authoritative method capability metadata is unavailable",
158:            )
159:        })?;
160:    let required = method_capability.required_capability;
161:    let identity = identity
162:        .filter(|identity| !identity.principal_id.is_empty() && !identity.session_id.is_empty())
163:        .ok_or_else(|| {
164:            capability_denied(
165:                plugin_id,
166:                method_name,
167:                Some(&required),
168:                "authenticated request identity is unavailable",
169:            )
170:        })?;
171:    let capability_matches = capability_id == Some(required.as_str());
172:    let principal_grants = load_capability_grants(&identity.principal_id).contains(&required);
173:
174:    if capability_matches && principal_grants {
175:        Ok(())
176:    } else {
177:        Err(capability_denied(
178:            plugin_id,
179:            method_name,
180:            Some(&required),
181:            "matching request capability and exact-principal grant are required",
182:        ))
183:    }
184:}

content.text:
Root cause found — verified end to end. And you were right to push "fix it right": my grant shortcut would have been a no-op, because there's nothing to grant.

**The gate, verified in source** (`grpc_server.rs:143-184`): the required capability comes from the *sealed schema*, the client's header must equal it, and the principal's grants must contain it. Missing method metadata → deny. The UI's denial is that third case.

**UI expects vs backend seals:**

| UI calls (`chat_response` door) | Sealed? | Dispatched? |
|---|---|---|
| `start_conversation` (read) | ✅ | ✅ dispatch arm |
| `submit_turn` (`chat_response.submit`) | ❌ no such method | ❌ zero hits in bridge |
| `get_turn_response` (read) | ✅ | ✅ dispatch arm |
| `get_doorbell` | ❌ no such method | via Subscribe path instead |

The human-submit leg exists *inside* the engine (`commit_human_turn` — needs `chat_response.read`, reachable only through native `open_chat_turn` from the mount/attach path). The Oct 30 UI was built against a `submit_turn` the backend never sealed — that's the skew, not a missing grant. `chat_response.submit` appears nowhere server-side, so writing it into the grants doc would have changed nothing. The blockers earned their keep.

**True fix-right scope:**
1. Plugin: add `submit_turn` to `METHODS` + typed Input/Output + `required_capability` arm + dispatch arm wired to `commit_human_turn` + tests (bridge + plugin)
2. Build → seal → golden release → activate
3. Grant the new cap to `1262e982-…` in the durable doc (materializer projects it)
4. Verify with one turn, keep the receipt

Blockers standing in the way: both trees dirty (9 conflicted UI files here, modified platform files there), release-kit digest mismatch blocking the launcher, and seal/activate needing sudo + restarts.

Advisory validated — my "wire it to `commit_human_turn`" would have skipped five load-bearing guards. Corrected plan:

`open_chat_turn` enforces, in order: verified human session → responder holds `chat_response.respond` → conversation in the principal's scope → pending reservation first (one open turn per conversation, serializes) → responder wake → human commit → index match (`human.turn_index + 1 == pending`), cancelling the reservation on any mismatch or error. A thin wrapper around `commit_human_turn` drops all of that except the read-grant check.

So the dispatch arm for `submit_turn` must call **`open_chat_turn`**, reusing the `attach` path's responder selection (`OP_CONTROL_PLANE_CHATBOT_PRINCIPAL_ID`) — one open question I won't decide unilaterally: personal-mode turns, same designated responder or mode-routed? Default is the attach path's choice unless you say otherwise.

Then build → seal → release → grant → one-turn verify, with the dirty-tree and digest blockers still standing.
